\begin{abstract}
Encrypted traffic classifiers are routinely reported at 95--99\% accuracy. We
show that on one of two public corpora, the same model and the same code score
macro-F1 \textbf{0.992} under the evaluation protocol standard in the
literature and \textbf{0.574} under a protocol that keeps correlated flows
apart. Nothing changes but the partition.

The inflation is not a property of random splitting as such. On a second
corpus, random, session-disjoint and temporal splitting are indistinguishable,
while \emph{server}-disjoint splitting costs 0.19 macro-F1. The axis that
matters is whichever grouping the label is nearly a function of, and it differs
by how the corpus was collected. Controlling the wrong axis protects nothing.

We give a diagnostic that identifies the right axis before any model is
trained: single-identifier probes. On the first corpus a decision tree on the
\emph{server address alone} reaches 0.999 under a random split; on the second,
the \emph{SNI string alone} reaches 0.967 under every split, which is roughly
the ceiling of the labelling process itself.

We then evaluate a metric-trained flow embedding under the strict protocols,
against eight classical and four deep baselines on identical committed splits.
It leads every deep baseline but not gradient-boosted trees on twenty packet
sizes. Five of our own architectural claims fail their own pre-registered
tests, including the one we expected to survive: distance-based rejection of
unknown applications beats softmax thresholding by a wide margin, but ablating
\emph{every} metric objective makes rejection \emph{better}, so the advantage
belongs to the rejection rule rather than to the training.

All splits, results and negative findings are released.
\end{abstract}

\keywords{encrypted traffic classification, evaluation methodology, QUIC,
          traffic analysis, measurement}
